name: Battle on the Ice
info: The united forces of Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal under Prince Alexander Nevsky defeated the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Dorpat under Bishop Hermann of Dorpat at Lake Peipus on 5 April 1242, a battle later made a Russian national symbol.

facts.place: The frozen Lake Peipus; the Novgorod First Chronicle names Uzmen, by the Raven's Rock. Where on the lake, or beside it, is disputed
facts.sides: Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal under Prince Alexander Nevsky, around 5,000 men by David Nicolle's conservative estimate; the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Dorpat under Bishop Hermann of Dorpat, around 2,600 by the same estimate
facts.outcome: Alexander's forces won. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle gives twenty Brothers dead and six captured; the Novgorod First Chronicle gives 400 Germans dead and fifty taken, with a countless number of Estonians killed.

t: Estimates of the armies vary widely among scholars; David Nicolle's conservative figures are around 5,000 Novgorodians against around 2,600 crusaders.
None of the primary sources says the ice broke or that knights drowned; Donald Ostrowski concludes that this image first appeared in Eisenstein's film of 1938.
Russian historiography has treated the battle as significant for the balance between Western Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy, but whether it was a crusade, and how large it was, is disputed.
dyk: The earliest account of the battle, the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, says the dead fell 'on the grass'; the Life of Alexander Nevsky, from the mid-15th century, was the first version to place the battle on the ice itself.

sections.background:
The origins of the conflict are unclear and controversial. An influential historiographical tradition links it to three earlier clashes in which Aleksandr Yaroslavich was involved: the alleged Battle of the Neva of July 1240, attested only in Rus' sources, the Izborsk and Pskov campaign of September 1240, and the Votia campaign of winter 1240–1241. If the Battle of the Neva took place, it was probably only a minor clash in which religion played no role.

Novgorodians had tried to subjugate, raid and convert the pagan Estonians, known as Chud', since 1030, when they established the outpost of Yuryev, modern Tartu. The Livonian Brothers of the Sword captured Yuryev in 1224, and it became the capital of the Bishopric of Dorpat. Yaroslav, son of Vladimir Mstislavich of Pskov, tried with the help of his brother-in-law Bishop Hermann of Dorpat to become prince of Pskov, failing in 1233 and succeeding in September 1240.

In the winter of 1240–1241 the Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek and the Livonian Order launched the Votia campaign, which may properly be considered a crusade in the sense of a missionary conquest of 'pagan' lands. The Sword Brothers and Bishop Henry of Ösel–Wiek probably did not intend to attack Novgorod, but their actions provoked a Novgorodian counterattack in 1241, delayed by internal strife in Novgorod. Alexander retook Votia and Pskov and continued into Estonian-German territory. In the spring of 1242 the Teutonic Knights defeated a detachment of his army about 20 kilometres (12 mi) south of Dorpat, and Alexander set up a position at Lake Peipus.
sections.forces:
The united forces of the Republic of Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal, led by Prince Alexander Nevsky, faced the forces of the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Dorpat, led by Bishop Hermann of Dorpat. Estimates of the numbers vary widely among scholars. A more conservative estimate by David Nicolle (1996) puts the crusader forces at around 2,600: 800 Danish and German knights, 100 Teutonic knights, 300 Danes, 400 Germans and 1,000 Estonian infantry. The Novgorodians fielded around 5,000 men: the bodyguards (druzhina) of Alexander and his brother Andrei, around 1,000 in all, plus 2,000 Novgorod militia, 1,400 Finno-Ugrian tribesmen and 600 horse archers.

The chronicles of the two sides describe the armies differently. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, written in the 1290s, says that Bishop Henry's men had brought too few people and that the Brothers' army was too small, but that they decided to attack the Rus'. It says the Rus' had many archers and so many troops that there were easily sixty men for every German knight. The Laurentian continuation of the Suzdalian Chronicle says that Grand Prince Iaroslav sent his son Andrei to Novgorod in aid of Alexander against the Germans.

According to the Novgorod First Chronicle, Alexander and all the men of Novgorod drew up their forces by the lake, at Uzmen, by the Raven's Rock, and the Germans and the Estonians rode at them, driving themselves like a wedge through their army.
sections.course:
In the reconstruction given by scholars, the Teutonic knights and crusaders charged across the lake and reached the enemy, but were held up by the infantry of the Novgorodian militia, which slowed the momentum of the attack. The battle was fierce, with the allied Rus' soldiers fighting the Teutonic and crusader troops on the frozen surface of the lake. After a little more than two hours of close quarters fighting, Alexander ordered the left and right wings of his army, including cavalry, into the battle. The crusaders were by then exhausted from the constant struggle on the slippery surface. They began to retreat in disarray deeper onto the ice, and the appearance of the fresh Novgorod cavalry made them retreat in panic.

The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle tells it from the Order's side. The battle began with a bold assault in front of the king's men, and the Brothers' banners were soon flying in the midst of the archers, while swords were heard cutting helmets apart. Many from both sides fell dead on the grass. Then the Brothers' army was completely surrounded and, although the Brothers fought well enough, they were cut down. Some of those from Dorpat escaped, and it was their salvation that they had been forced to flee.

The Novgorod First Chronicle speaks of a great slaughter of Germans and Estonians and says the fighting continued during the pursuit on the ice, seven versts short of the Subol shore.
sections.aftermath:
The two sides' chronicles give different losses. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle says that twenty Brothers lay dead and six were captured. The Synod Scroll of the Novgorod First Chronicle says that a countless number of Estonians fell, and 400 of the Germans, and that fifty were taken with their hands and brought to Novgorod. The Younger Redaction of that chronicle, compiled in the 1440s, raised the number of Germans killed from 400 to 500. The Laurentian continuation says that the Germans were defeated and many prisoners taken, and that Andrei returned to his father with honour.

The tradition holds that the knights' defeat prevented the crusaders from retaking Pskov, the linchpin of their eastern crusade, and so halted the eastward expansion of the Teutonic Order. On this view the river Narva and Lake Peipus then represented a stable boundary dividing Eastern Orthodoxy from Western Catholicism.

The revisionist historian John L. I. Fennell argued in 1983 that the apparently low number of knights' casualties according to their own sources indicates how small the encounter was, and that most of the Teutonic Knights were by then engaged elsewhere in the Baltic.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from four main accounts, none of them written at the time. The Livonian Rhymed Chronicle of the Livonian Order was written in the 1290s. The Laurentian continuation of the Suzdalian Chronicle was compiled in 1377, though its entry may have been composed around 1310. The Synod Scroll of the Novgorod First Chronicle has an entry dated to about 1350, and the Younger Redaction was compiled in the 1440s. The Life of Alexander Nevsky, whose earliest redaction Donald Ostrowski dated to the mid-15th century, combined elements of the Laurentian, Novgorod and Rostov-Suzdal accounts.

The details grew with the accounts. Ostrowski argues that the earliest account says the dead fell on the grass and the Laurentian continuation places the fighting at a lake beyond Pskov, not on it. Only decades later was a specific lake named and the Livonians said to be chased across its ice, and only in the 15th century did the Life place the battle itself on the ice. No primary source mentions the ice breaking.

In 1958 and 1959 underwater investigations in the northern part of Lake Lämmi, where some Soviet researchers presumed the combat happened, found no artefacts of the battle. Ostrowski commented that this was to be expected, as the sources do not say that the ice broke and many soldiers drowned. Fennell claimed that neither the Laurentian chronicle nor any Swedish source mentions the occasion; Ostrowski pointed out that the Laurentian Codex does mention it in passing but gives only minimal information.
sections.legacy:
Russian historiography has traditionally interpreted the outcome as significant for the balance of power between Western Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy. It is disputed whether the battle should be called a crusade, and whether it was a significant defeat for Catholic forces in the Northern Crusades. Anti Selart asserts that the crusades were not an attempt to conquer Rus' but were still an attack on Novgorod's territory and interests, and notes that the papal bulls of 1240 to 1243 speak of warfare against non-Christians, not against Russians. Gustav A. Donner argued in 1929 that the Baltic campaigns were coordinated from the Roman Curia; more recent historians reject a papal master plan for want of decisive evidence.

Macarius of Moscow canonised Alexander Nevsky as a saint of the Russian Orthodox Church in 1547. Sergei Eisenstein's film Alexander Nevsky, released in 1938, created a popular image of the battle that is often mistaken for the real events, including knights drowning as the ice breaks. Jerry Smith and William Urban, editors of the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle in English, wrote that the film tells more about 1939 than 1242.

During the Second World War Nevsky became a national Soviet Russian symbol of the struggle against German occupation, and the Order of Alexander Nevsky was established as a military award in 1942. The Russian Federation commemorates the victory as one of the Days of Military Honour, and in 2010 its government amended the order's statute to make it an award for excellent civilian service.

summary: On 5 April 1242 Alexander Nevsky's Novgorodian and Vladimir-Suzdal army defeated the Livonian Order and the Bishopric of Dorpat at Lake Peipus. Its size and importance are disputed, and later Russian tradition made it a symbol of Orthodox and national resistance.

Mari Isoaho, The Image of Aleksandr Nevskiy in Medieval Russia: Warrior and Saint (Brill, 2006)

notes: The article's own make-up is thin on the fighting: the course section combines Nicolle-style reconstruction (no named source for the two-hour phase) with the chronicles' accounts.

The article gives no present-day country for the lake and does not say the site is disputed; facts.place says 'disputed' only because the sources differ (on the ice, at a lake beyond Pskov, Uzmen) and Soviet researchers presumed Lake Lämmi. Editor to check.
The 'sixty men for every German knight' is the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle's own claim.
The article's 'Votia campaign' text mixes Livonian Order and Sword Brothers; kept as given.
Left out: the Swedish motives and the 1237 papal letter to Uppsala, the Battle of Liubech of 1016 (Ostrowski's influence on Eisenstein).
Lead says 'Bishop Hermann of Dorpat' led the Livonian side while the chronicle names Bishop Henry's men; both kept as stated.
